laws-murphys-law: Named for aerospace engineer Edward A. Murphy Jr. The name is generally traced to rocket sled tests at Muroc Army Air Field (later Edwards Air Force Base) in 1948 or 1949, after a mishap. Murphy's own wording was closer to: if there are two or more ways to do something and one of them ends in catastrophe, someone will do it that way. The short form reached the public through a press conference held by project leader John Paul Stapp.
laws-hofstadters-law: Coined by Douglas Hofstadter in Godel, Escher, Bach (1979). The self-reference is the joke: padding your estimate does not fix it.
laws-parkinsons-law: The opening observation of a satirical essay by naval historian C. Northcote Parkinson, published in The Economist on 19 November 1955, two days after a Royal Commission report on the British Civil Service.
laws-hanlons-razor: Printed as Hanlon's razor in Arthur Bloch's Murphy's Law Book Two (1980), submitted by a Robert J. Hanlon about whom nothing else is known. Similar sentiments appear earlier, in H. G. Wells's The Wheels of Chance (1896) and Robert Heinlein's Logic of Empire (1941). The name echoes Occam's razor.
laws-sturgeons-law: Theodore Sturgeon wrote in his September 1957 Venture Science Fiction column that science fiction is ninety percent crud, but so is ninety percent of everything. He restated it in 1958 as: Ninety percent of everything is crud.
laws-occams-razor: Named for the 14th century friar William of Ockham, who never wrote this sentence. Its familiar form is credited to the Irish Franciscan John Punch in 1639, who called it a common axiom of the Scholastics. Ockham's own versions include that plurality must never be posited without necessity.
laws-goodharts-law: Economist Charles Goodhart expressed the core idea in a 1975 article on monetary policy: any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes. The short form is anthropologist Marilyn Strathern's 1997 rewording.
laws-galls-law: From John Gall's book on why systems fail, first published in 1975 as General Systemantics and reissued in 1977 as Systemantics. He adds that a complex system designed from scratch never works and cannot be patched up to make it work, so you have to start over with a working simple system.
laws-chestertons-fence: From Chesterton's 1929 book The Thing. He imagines a reformer who finds a fence or gate across a road and wants it cleared away because he cannot see its use. The wiser reformer, he says, should answer with the lines quoted here.
laws-the-peter-principle: Formulated from the research of Laurence J. Peter and published in 1969 under both names, though Raymond Hull wrote almost all of the text. The book also states the corollary that in time every post tends to be occupied by an employee who is incompetent to carry out its duties.
laws-brandolinis-law: Coined by Italian programmer Alberto Brandolini, who posted it on Twitter in January 2013.
laws-hicks-law: Named for psychologist William Edmund Hick, who began his reaction-time experiments in 1951 and published them in 1952, and for Ray Hyman, whose related paper followed in 1953. It is also called the Hick-Hyman law.
laws-the-pareto-principle: Economist Vilfredo Pareto noticed that about 80 percent of Italy's land was owned by 20 percent of the population. In 1941 quality engineer Joseph Juran developed it into a general rule for quality control, later calling it the vital few and the useful many.
laws-finagles-law: Often credited to Astounding Science Fiction editor John W. Campbell Jr. One of the earliest records is a December 1962 article, Finagle Factors, in The Michigan Technic, credited to Campbell under the byline I. Finaglin. The usual printed form has a dash before the last clause; a comma is used here.
laws-segals-law: The saying first ran in the San Diego Union on 20 September 1930, in a longer item about jewelers advising men to carry two watches. It was later wrongly credited to radio man Lee Segall, and Arthur Bloch's Murphy's Law books spelled the name Segal.
laws-conways-law: From Melvin Conway's paper How Do Committees Invent?, published in Datamation in April 1968. The sentence quoted is the paper's own statement of its basic thesis.
laws-brookss-law: Coined by Fred Brooks in his 1975 book The Mythical Man-Month.
laws-cunninghams-law: Steven McGeady named it in a May 2010 post on The New York Times' Schott's Vocab blog, describing advice Ward Cunningham gave him in the early 1980s. Cunningham himself calls it a misquote that disproves itself by propagating through the internet and says he never suggested asking questions by posting wrong answers.
laws-betteridges-law-of-headlines: British technology journalist Ian Betteridge wrote in a February 2009 article that this was his maxim for headlines that end in a question mark.
laws-the-lindy-effect: Named for Lindy's deli in New York, where comedians gathered. Albert Goldman used the idea about television comedians in a 1964 article in The New Republic, Benoit Mandelbrot gave a version in 1982, and Nassim Nicholas Taleb extended it to technologies and ideas in Antifragile (2012).
laws-amaras-law: Coined in 1978 by Roy Amara, an American researcher and futurist who was president of the Institute for the Future.
laws-kernighans-law: From the second edition of The Elements of Programming Style by Brian Kernighan and P. J. Plauger (first edition 1974, second edition 1978), chapter 2. The shorter form often quoted, that debugging is twice as hard as writing the code in the first place, compresses this passage.
laws-the-law-of-triviality: Stated by C. Northcote Parkinson in Parkinson's Law and Other Studies in Administration (1957). His illustration is the bicycle shed, which everyone can picture, so it draws the most debate. Also called bikeshedding.
laws-hitchenss-razor: Christopher Hitchens wrote it in God Is Not Great (2007), in a passage about miracles. It echoes the older Latin maxim Quod gratis asseritur, gratis negatur: what is freely asserted is freely denied.
laws-campbells-law: From social psychologist Donald T. Campbell's paper Assessing the impact of planned social change, published in Evaluation and Program Planning in 1979. Similar in spirit to Goodhart's law.
laws-sayres-law: Named for Columbia University political scientist Wallace Sayre. His colleague Herbert Kaufman dates the idea to the early 1950s and says Sayre usually put it as: the politics of the university are so intense because the stakes are so low. The wording here is the version credited to Charles Issawi.
laws-the-law-of-the-instrument: Written by Abraham Maslow in The Psychology of Science (1966). Abraham Kaplan had stated the idea in 1964 as: give a small boy a hammer, and he will find that everything he encounters needs pounding.
laws-stiglers-law-of-eponymy: Statistician Stephen Stigler stated it in a 1980 paper in Transactions of the New York Academy of Sciences, a Festschrift for Robert K. Merton.
laws-the-ninety-ninety-rule: Credited to Tom Cargill of Bell Labs and popularized by Jon Bentley in his September 1985 Programming Pearls column in Communications of the ACM, where it was called the Rule of Credibility. The numbers add up to 180 percent on purpose.
laws-greshams-law: Named after Tudor financier Sir Thomas Gresham, who in a 1558 letter to Queen Elizabeth wrote that good and bad coin cannot circulate together. The name Gresham's law dates only to 1858, when economist Henry Dunning Macleod gave it.
laws-cipollas-first-law-of-stupidity: The first of five laws in economic historian Carlo M. Cipolla's 1976 essay The Basic Laws of Human Stupidity, written in Italian and later collected in Allegro ma non troppo (1988).
laws-wiios-first-law: From Finnish communication scholar Osmo A. Wiio, in his 1978 book Wiion lait, ja vahan muidenkin (Wiio's laws, and some others of the same kind).
laws-the-sagan-standard: Popularized by Carl Sagan, who used it in Cosmos (1980) and stated it in a 1977 interview. Sociologist Marcello Truzzi had written that extraordinary claims require extraordinary proof in 1975 and 1978. David Hume and Pierre-Simon Laplace made similar points earlier.
laws-the-shirky-principle: Kevin Kelly named it the Shirky Principle in April 2010, crediting Clay Shirky, because the phrasing reminded him of the clarity of the Peter Principle.
laws-tanstaafl: The phrase was in use by the 1930s and its first appearance is unknown. An early use in the current sense is Walter Morrow's 1938 fable Economics in Eight Words in the El Paso Herald-Post. Robert Heinlein's 1966 novel The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress made the acronym TANSTAAFL a central theme and brought it to wide use.
